adCopy: Exiled. Disowned. Arrested for defending herself. Elena was supposed to stay broken. Instead, she defeats two hunters, removes three silver bullets, and saves the most powerful Alpha heir alive. They called the white wolf cursed—now she’s coming back. 👑🔥 Chapter 1: What the Moon Returned Elena "Smash!" The plate struck the tile and burst, scattering porcelain in every direction. Conversation vanished. Forks stalled near open mouths, and the entire cafe seemed to hold its breath. My hands remained outstretched, shaking above the wreckage. Of course. One more failure to prove I belonged nowhere, including this ordinary human world where everyone acted as though living came easily. "Grant." My manager sharpened my name into a weapon. "What is wrong with you this time?" Whatever answer he wanted, I didn't have it. "I'll take care of this." I crouched and gathered the fragments. Their edges opened my palms, leaving bright beads of blood along the cuts. The pain gave me something solid to focus on, unlike the vacant place inside my chest where my wolf should have been. Keep the mask on. Draw a breath. Fall apart somewhere else. "Then clean every piece," he snapped. "I don't want to come back here." My eyes stayed on the floor. He wouldn't get to watch the humiliation reach my face. Exile had begun three years ago, yet I still moved through every room like a spirit borrowing someone else's body. Once the shards were in the trash, I tore away my apron and left before another insult could follow me through the door. Rain glazed the street outside, pulling the neon into long, bruised streaks. The wind sliced through my jacket, but weather couldn't frighten me. I'd survived far worse, even after losing my wolf. With both hands buried in my pockets, I headed toward my bike. The drunk who haunted the corner lurched into my path. "There she is, the wild one." His gaze crawled over me as he reached for my waist. "All done working? I'll get you a drink." My pulse jumped as I retreated. "Find someone else." He caught my wrist before I could turn. "Come on, sweetheart. I've been watching you the whole night. There's something strange about you. Something dangerous." Hot, sour breath washed over my face when he leaned in. "Dangerous is exactly what I like." A deeper voice than mine seemed to rise from my throat. "Take your hand off me." His grin widened. "You take it off." Fine. I drove my fist into his chest. He flew backward, struck a table, and landed amid crash of broken glass. "She jumped me!" he screamed from the pavement. "That psycho bitch attacked me!" A ring of space opened around us. People raised their phones, recording through luminous screens, while my manager appeared in the entrance with rage draining the color from his face. Someone in the crowd shouted, "Call the police!" Within minutes, an officer forced me into a patrol car. Through the window, I saw the drunk smiling like the verdict had already gone his way. Bleach and old coffee fouled the air in the interrogation room. Across the table, Officer Daniel watched me rub the cuff marks circling my wrists. "You're twenty-one," he said, asking for confirmation a third time. "I am." "There's no guardian responsible for you?" "No." "And you have no family?" "None." I'd repeated that lie for so many years that it had become easier to wear than the truth. The door swung inward. Each click of approaching heels sounded expensive, precise, and absolute. My mother, Vanessa Grant, entered. She completed the release paperwork without once looking at me. Her attention found me only after we stepped outside, when her hand flashed up and struck my cheek. "You disappear for three years, then announce your return like this?" she hissed. "I have to collect you from a human police station as if you're some street criminal." Shock held my fingers against the burning skin. "That's not what happened." "I didn't ask you to talk." Contempt made her stare colder than the night. "They expelled you for good reason. Exile clearly taught you nothing. You're a stain, Elena, and stain belongs out of sight." Already finished with me, she glanced at her watch. "Your grandfather expects you at home. Stop forcing me to spend my time fixing your disasters." Understanding landed harder than her slap. "You only came because Walter ordered you to." Not a muscle shifted in her face. "Lock yourself away tonight. The full moon is here." A bitter laugh escaped me. "You know perfectly well that my wolf abandoned me three years ago." I returned to my Ducati and brought the engine roaring to life. Vanessa remained on the curb as I accelerated away, smearing the city's red and gold lights behind me. Beyond the outskirts, the road opened through the darkness like a waiting mouth. I pushed the bike faster while the wind clawed at my clothes. Above the trees, the moon lomed white and swollen. For three years, I'd carried that dead space inside me. At every full moon, I'd waited for my wolf to come back, clinging to the hope that I could prove everyone wrong about white wolves being cursed. Each time, the night had given me nothing. I twisted the throttle farther, trying to leave my thoughts behind. Then a figure appeared beside the road. A man lay blood-soaked beneath the moon's silver light. Two armed shapes stood over him, and silver flashed from their weapons. Hunters. Every sense I had tightened. Leaving would have been smarter. Instead, the wounded man's thin but stubborn breathing pulled me off the bike. I shut down the engine and moved quietly among the trees. One hunter spun toward the sound. Recognition became a smile. "You weren't supposed to witness this." A silver round whispered beside my ear. Survival seized control, not my wolf, because she was still gone. I crashed into him, wrenched away his gun, and drove him into the ground. The island had drilled the same lesson into me three years earlier: kill first or die. I faced the injured stranger, fighting for breath. "This had better worth the trouble." He was tall and powerfully built, and even half-dead, he seemed to press against the space around him. No human carried an aura like that. Pine resin, wet soil, and something keenly alive filled my nose as I searched his side for the wound. The instant my fingertips touched him, his body jerked. One hand snapped around my wrist. Heat detonated beneath my skin, racing up my arm as if a flame had been dragged across the bone. Impossible. No. It couldn't be. Not now. I tore myself free, but the change had already started. My nails had split apart, the skin around them drawing taut while rough white fur forced its way through. Words deserted me. Despite the blood covering him, the stranger's eyes opened with sudden clarity. Storm-grey and fierce, they fixed on mine. What emerged from his throat scarcely sounded human. "Mine." His claim barely reached me. I could only stare as white fur raced over my skin with the hunger of spreading fire. Three years. I'd marked every day of them. For three years, I'd existed as half of myself. People had told me it might better this way, that perhaps losing her had made me safer. I'd swallowed every protest until silence tasted like blood rather than let them hear me rage at the injustice. Now my wolf was moving inside me again, uncoiling as though she had finally awakened from a sleep without end. Her return carried the person I used to be back with it. They had been wrong about more than they knew. I would not remain their victim. Chapter 2: Poison Beneath the Moon Elena The force inside me had been on the verge of swallowing me whole. Then, without warning, the wolf beneath my skin retreated into complete silence. I stared at the wounded stranger. "What just happened?" The question escaped under my breath, meant more for me than for him. No reply came. His breaths barely disturbed his chest, and the silver was already coursing through his body. From each wound, darkened veins were spreading beneath his skin. A human emergency room would have no way to save him. Above us, the full moon shone with brutal clarity. I looked from it to the werewolf dying on the pavement. Leaving was the sensible choice, particularly on this night, yet my feet refused to move. Perhaps what had happened moments ago demanded an explanation. Or maybe I possessed more conscience than sense. "Damn it." The decision settled heavily in my stomach. "You'd better worth the trouble." The two shooters I'd knocked unconscious still lay where they had fallen. After confirming neither had stirred, I sent their silver-loaded guns skidding out of reach and hauled the injured man toward my motorcycle. Getting him onto the bike almost toppled us more than once. He saged against my back, utterly limp, while I started the engine. I hooked one arm around his waist so he wouldn't slide onto the road. Portland University's medical lab was my only option. As a student in the medical program, I'd spent more late nights there than I could count, conducting private research into why my wolf had been suppressed. Nowhere else offered both the instruments and the materials necessary to treat him. Every crack and dip in the pavement dragged a groan from him. The university grounds had gone quiet by the time we arrived. My key card opened the research building's service entrance, and from there I supported and dragged him through vacant hallways until we reached the lab. Once the door was locked behind us, I switched only the dimest lights. Along the rear wall, hidden from casual inspection, waited my private collection of werewolf medicine: research journals, preserved samples, and specialized tools I'd designed for silver injuries. Outcasts did enjoy one small privilege. Nobody cared enough to question my schedule or the peculiar direction of my work. I wrestled him onto the examination table and ripped apart his blood-drenched shirt. Three bullet holes marked his torso. The tissue surrounding them had turned black, while poisoned veins continued branching outward in thin, ugly webs. The silver poisoning had already reached an advanced stage. If it touched his heart, he was finished, and I estimated he had less than an hour. I had barely arranged my instruments when his eyes snapped open. A hand shot around my neck before I could retreat, and his fingers crushed into my throat. Injured or not, this wolf was far from helpless. "Who are you?" A vivid electric blue flashed through his eyes. "Where have you taken me?" Air came painfully, but I kept my face composed. "Unless you've suddenly decided to die, release me. Those silver rounds are poisoning you, and no one else here can remove them." Instead of loosening, his grip grew tighter. "Why would I put my life in the hands of a wolf who barely carries a scent?" The words struck deeper than they should have. My wolf had fallen silent again, exactly as she had remained for the past three years. I refused to give him the satisfaction of seeing the wound he'd opened. "Had I wanted you dead, I would have abandoned you beside the road." I held his stare. "Let me work and survive, or keep choking me and die. Decide." Suspicion hardened his expression. "You expect me to ignore the deception I can smell on you? What aren't you telling me?" "At this moment, I'm concealing how badly you're irritating me." I didn't look away. "You're soaking my laboratory in blood, and explaining your corpse to campus security tomorrow isn't on my schedule." Whatever heard in my answer finally persuaded him. His fingers withdrew from my throat, and he collapsed against the table with a strained grunt. I reached for the forceps I'd built for this exact purpose. "This is going to hurt. Not a little." For the next hour, I shut out everything except the work. Childhood memories guided my hands, images of my grandmother practicing medicine while I watched beside her. That had been before my exile, when the Mercy Pack was still my home and she had been teaching me all she knew. One after another, I removed the three silver bullets buried inside him. He never cried out. Sweat gathered across his brow, however, and his jaw stayed clenched with enough force to break a tooth. His restraint deserved respect; another werewolf would have been howling long before then. The rounds had driven deep into the muscle and stopped dangerously near vital organs. With careful, practiced movements, I cut poisoned flesh away from healthy tissue and searched each wound for lethal fragments. "One more," I said quietly. The third bullet had lodged close to his heart, forcing me to probe farther than I liked. The moment my forceps finally drew it free, pain overwhelmed him and he lost consciousness. After cleaning the wounds, I bandaged them and measured his vital signs again. His heartbeat had strengthened, and the black tracery beneath his skin was already receding. He would survive, though the poisoning would leave him weak for several days. With him unconscious, I searched for a phone someone else could take responsibility for him. An expensive smartphone turned up in his jacket. I unlocked the recent-call list and selected the number appearing most often. A man picked up almost immediately. "Boss, where are you? We've been searching for hours!" "Your boss was shot in Portland," I replied. "He is stable now, but he hasn't regained consciousness. You'll find him in the medical research lab at Portland University." "What? Who am I speaking to?" he demanded. I ended the call without identifying myself. While returning the phone, I checked the remaining pockets. A wallet slipped loose, followed by a business card stamped in gold: DAMIAN HAYES CEO, HAYES ENTERPRISES ALPHA, BLODFANG PACK My hand stopped. The small card seemed to gain weight between my fingers. Damian Hayes was the Alpha King's son, heir to the authority that controlled every western pack. The memory of my exile had never truly faded, and now it slammed into me with physical force. I was standing before the Pack Council again, listening as my sister Kendra tearfully claimed I'd lost control and attacked human. My mother's eyes had remained cold while she disowned me. Through it all, Damian Hayes had watched without emotion as the council stripped away my territory rights and Pack protection. Biterness rose hot in my throat as I studied the unconscious man. Out of every werewolf who might have bled across that road tonight, I had saved him. Engines rumbled somewhere beyond the building, drawing closer. His people were arriving. I moved quickly, collecting my equipment and research notes until nothing remained that could expose the lab's connection to werewolf medicine. At the door, I allowed myself one final glance at him. Why was he the one who woke my wolf? Chapter 3: The Silver-Eyed Healer Blood coated my tongue with the taste of rust. Beneath it lurked the chemical sting of antiseptic. Those two sensations hauled me awake before the pain arrived, a white-hot current spreading through my chest as though liquid silver had entered my bloodstream. I forced my eyelids apart. Fluorescent panels glared overhead, and stainless-stel equipment surrounded the narrow table beneath me. A medical laboratory, not a hospital. "Mr. Hayes, you're conscious. Thank God." Justin emerged beside the table while my vision steadied. Worry had carved lines across my security chief's face, and his loosened tie hung crooked over a shirt that was normally immaculate. Bracing one hand against the table, I attempted to sit. A vicious stab through my torso stopped me. Three precisely wrapped dressings covered my wounds. My throat scraped when I spoke. "Where are the bullets?" "They've been removed." Justin indicated a steel tray where three silver rounds rested. "Someone operated on you here. You were already alone by the time we traced your phone and reached the lab." Broken images surfaced without forming a complete memory. Silver eyes. A strange certainty that I was safe. Something pale moving at the edge of my sight - fur, perhaps, and white. Yet the scent troubled me most. It had been so faint it should have vanished beneath the blood and disinfectant, but some primitive part of me had recognized it. I still couldn't explain what it had awakened. I shut my eyes and tried to catch the woman's face again. "She had silver eyes, and almost no scent. What I did smell reminded me of smoke." Looking at Justin, I hardened my voice. "Find her. I want every available detail." "Shouldn't the people who tried to kill you come first, sir?" One glance silenced the concern in his expression. "I don't need anyone to remind me that an assassination attempt requires investigation. You have two priorities: identify the shooters and locate the woman who kept me alive. Handle both. Immediately." Justin pulled himself upright. "Understood. Teams are already pursuing the gunmen." "Then take me to the Center." I lowered my feet to the floor despite the protest from every injured muscle. "Malcolm needs to examine these wounds." A harmless wellness clinic on Seattle's outskirts concealed the Silvershining Moon Medical Center underground. Justin supported me through its restricted entrance, where Dr. Malcolm had been waiting after receiving an advance report. He greeted me with a deferential dip of his head. "Alpha Hayes. Let me see what was done." Inside an immaculate examination room, Malcolm unwound the dressings and exposed the sutures. The higher his eyebrows rose, the more closely he leaned over my chest. "Remarkable," he murmured. "I haven't encountered technique this refined since Alpha Ingrid was alive." I tracked every change in his face. "What does that tell you?" "Not a trace of silver toxicity remains in the nearby tissue. The extraction was flawless." Astonishment lingered in Malcolm's voice as he shook his head. "Your surgeon possessed rare skill and highly specialized training. Whoever it was understood precisely how silver damages our bodies and how to neutralize its effects." Another fragment of the operation refused to leave me alone. While she had worked, my wolf had calmed completely, soothed by her presence rather than restrained by force. Healing might explain it. Comfort did not. I'd never experienced that kind of peace, and remembering it disturbed me. "Does anyone in Seattle have that level of knowledge?" Malcolm held my gaze. "No one has since the Mercy Pack's Alpha died years ago. Their healing practices died with him." His expression tightened. "Our territorial conflicts have become especially costly because too few capable healers remain." I stored the connection for later: the Mercy Pack, an exceptional healer, and white wolf. The evidence still refused to assemble into a coherent answer. Once were in the rear of my Bentley, Justin passed me a tablet. "We've checked the laboratory access records and all nearby surveillance footage." I moved through the report until a photograph stopped my hand. Porcelain-pale skin framed a young woman's face, but her silver-gray eyes dominated it. Distance and defiance existed together in her expression. "Elena Grant," Justin said. "She's twenty-one and gifted medical student at Portland University." Cold slid through my veins. "Grant? Is she from the Mercy Pack?" "Yes. Walter Grant is her grandfather." He paused before continuing. "They exiled her three years ago, just after she turned eighteen and underwent her first shift." The information struck harder than expected. "The Grant exile should be in my memory. Why isn't it? Every official expulsion was supposed to cross my desk." "The family told the Council that she had lost control during her first transformation and attacked human. Their statement also alleged that she was collaborating with hostile forces." I returned to her photograph. Recognition seemed to hover beyond reach, scraping at the margins of my thoughts. By the following morning, Justin and I had arrived at Portland University. Students crossed the campus beyond the Bentley's tinted glass, drifting between buildings in loose groups. Then she appeared alone. Elena kept her silver eyes forward and walked with controlled grace, but vigilance sharpened every movement. I'd seen that same tension in wolves who had learned that danger might approach from behind. I spoke without raising my voice. "That's the woman. Bring here." Justin returned minutes later with Elena beside him. She entered the car and settled opposite me without hesitation, her face revealing nothing. "Mr. Hayes." Her cool greeting carried no surprise. At close range, I searched for some sign of the white wolf from my fractured memories. Her scent remained barely detectable, as if something had muted the werewolf within her. "Miss Grant." I offered her my business card. "HAYES ENTERPRISES has a medical research division. I want you to join it." Her eyebrow lifted a fraction. "What reason could you have for offering me that?" "Your ability is exceptional, and we require healers who can work at your level." "Your pack requires them," she corrected without warmth. "I want nothing to do with pack affairs." Rejection was unfamiliar enough to irritate me. "People would sacrifice almost anything for an opportunity like this." Elena met my stare directly, challenging an Alpha in a way few wolves would risk. "My life suits me as it is. I've learned how to survive without belonging to any pack." She reached for the door before I could answer. "If another silver bullet finds you, ask somebody else to sew you back together." After leaving the car, she crossed the pavement without a backward glance. My card fell from her fingers into a trash bin as casually as if it had never mattered. Silence stretched before Justin tested it. "Sir... she isn't like the other wolves." I kept watching until distance swallowed her. An unfamiliar force seemed to pull after her, magnetic and impossible to dismiss. In all my years, I'd never felt anything comparable. "Recover every record concerning the Grant family and the exile three years ago," I said at last. "Leave out nothing." Justin considered that. "You believe someone framed her?" My attention remained on the empty path outside. A dull ache widened in my chest, unrelated to the three bullet wounds. Beneath my skin, my wolf had grown agitated by Elena's departure, restless for reasons neither of us understood. "I don't know." The admission came quietly, even as my wolf continued to stir. "But I will find the truth.", Chapter 4: What Remained Elena From the steps of Portland University Medical School, I watched Damian's black Bentley turn the corner and vanish. Our encounter had left my pulse hammering. Now that he knew where I studied, regular visits and unwanted attention would probably follow. Last night's meeting had already awakened my awareness of his Alpha presence. His power tuged at me without permission, the way a magnet draws metal despite the distance between them. "So how am I supposed to stay away from him?" I shifted the bag digging into my shoulder. An Alpha's interest was the last complication I wanted, especially when that Alpha had watched my pack exile me without intervening. A vibration against my hip broke through my frustration. When I pulled out my phone, "Grandfather" glowed across the screen. Of everyone in my family, Walter Grant remained the sole person whose calls I was willing to answer. I hesitated before accepting. "Grandfather?" "Elena." Warmth softened his rough voice. "I've returned to Seattle." My anger loosened its grip. "How have you been feeling?" "Much better since coming home, but three years is too long to go without seeing you." Silence stretched briefly between us. "Please come back." With my eyes shut, I fought the emotions twisting through me. "Going back may not be wise." "The pack needs you, Elena. Please." Need me? Three years ago, they had thrown me out without mercy. Hearing that the pack suddenly required my presence would have been funny if the memory did not still hurt. Yet Walter's plea carried something that weakened my resistance. Returning for his sake was reason enough, and Seattle would place miles between Damian and me. "Okay," I said at last. "I'll drive there." Relief entered his voice. "That's my girl. I'll be here when you arrive." --- At my Moonlight Bay apartment, everything worth keeping fit inside one duffel. I packed my laptop, several outfits, and the medical equipment I depended on most. Necessity had long since made my life easy to move. Before leaving, I sent an encrypted notice to the Monglow Organization: [Aria temporarily offline. Relocating. Contact will resume once secure.] The motorcycle keys chilled my palm while I surveyed the nearly empty rooms. No memory here deserved sentiment. This apartment had never become a home; it had only given me somewhere to survive. Downstairs, a familiar SUV waited near the curb. My father, Jeremy Grant, was leaning against the driver's door, his tailored suit unable to hide his discomfort. He straightened when he saw me. "Your grandfather asked me to bring you home." "He didn't need to." I mounted my motorcycle and settled behind the handlebars. "I can find my own way. You all tried hard enough to erase that place from me, but I still remember the route." Jeremy's expression tightened. "You're only being permitted to return because your grandfather demanded it." "Thanks for clarifying the welcome." I started the engine and buried his next words beneath its growl. Rain had polished the highway into a dark ribbon beneath a colorless sky. With every mile north, Seattle announced itself more clearly through wet pine, cold air, and the faint animal musk marking werewolf land. I had traveled this road in the opposite direction three years earlier. Back then, tears had turned icy on my cheeks as I escaped the only home I had known. I had been eighteen, terrified, and blamed for losing control during my first transformation and attacking human. Wind battered my helmet now, but the motorcycle's wild power steadied me. "That frightened pup is gone," I told myself. My hands closed more firmly around the grips. I was returning by choice this time, not fleeing in fear. --- When the Grant estate emerged ahead, dread settled in my chest. Once, the property had displayed my family's strength with unmistakable pride. While Grandmother was still Alpha, everyone under her leadership had prospered. Little of that splendor remained. Tarnish duled the elaborate iron gates, weeds had swallowed the formerly perfect gardens, and no water ran through the central fountain. Only half the required security wolves patrolled the grounds. Those who had bothered to appear moved with the lazy indifference of wolves who expected no consequences. I stopped outside the main house and killed the motorcycle. In the sudden quiet, the estate seemed to hold its breath. My mother and sister waited at the entrance. Vanessa and Kendra Grant wore matching looks of disgust. Kendra's mouth twisted first. "The family's uncontrollable embarrassment has finally returned." Vanessa inspected my torn jeans and leather jacket as though both offended her personally. "Walter is in his study. He's expecting you." After removing my helmet, I shook my hair loose. "It's lovely seeing you too. Three years haven't improved either of you." I left them there and headed for the study. Time had barely touched the room. Ancient volumes about werewolf history still covered the walls, while old leather and pipe tobacco scented the air. The years had changed Walter more. Seated in his carved oak chair, he looked slighter than before; his face had gained deep lines, and his silver hair had thinned. Then he noticed me. His eyes, as bright and silver as mine, came alive. "There you are!" Rising quickly, he opened his arms. "My girl is home at last." I crossed the remaining distance and hugged him, taking comfort in the scent I remembered from childhood. "You've lost too much weight." "Meanwhile, you've become stronger." He drew back but kept his hands on my shoulders, studying my face. "Your eyes reveal it." Angry voices slipped through the closed door before I could answer. Vanessa and Kendra were discussing my return in the hallway, making no effort to lower their volume. "She remains dangerous," Kendra snapped. "During her first moon, she almost killed someone." My mother answered with colder restraint. "Allowing her back will damage our standing. The Pack will doubt your judgment, Walter." Fury darkened Grandfather's features. He crossed the study in several hard strides and yanked open the door. "That is enough!" The command in his voice belonged to the man who had built the Grant Pack from nothing. "Elena carries Grant blood. She is my granddaughter, and she has as much right to this territory as any member of this family." Silver fire sharpened his stare as he faced them. "In only three years, you've allowed our lands to decay. Security has become a joke, our investments are failing, and despite all of that, you still choose to attack one of your own?" Vanessa recoiled, while Kendra suddenly found the floor fascinating. Grandfather gave them no chance to respond. "Now that Elena has returned, she will continue her education at Crescendo Moon University Medical School." "They won't admit her," Vanessa objected. "Her expulsion was for violence. No reputable institution would overlook that." A scornful laugh escaped Kendra. "She's also missed three full years. Catching up would be impossible." I moved beside Grandfather. "I haven't missed them. I've completed three years of medical coursework in Portland, so transferring should present no problem." Pride replaced the anger on Walter's face. "Then I'll accompany you to registration tomorrow. No one there will dare turn away Grant." After I left the study, Vanessa and Kendra blocked me in the corridor. Kendra leaned closer, hostility tightening every word. "I don't know what you hope to gain by returning, but you will never become this family's Alpha. I've already ensured that." My mother's smile held no warmth. "A white-wolf abomination will never receive genuine acceptance from any Pack." Something within me fractured, but no rage spilled out. Instead, three years of isolation, pain, and fury compressed into an icy stillness. Silver light flashed through my vision as I advanced one deliberate step. "You framed a frightened girl and forced her out," I said quietly. "That girl no longer exists. Come after me again, and you'll learn exactly how much has changed. I promise neither of you will enjoy the lesson." Both women retreated before they could stop themselves. My wolf remained suppressed, yet they had sensed the difference in me: power had replaced fear, and I no longer needed their approval. Later, I stood at my bedroom window and studied the ruined beauty of the Grant estate. Three years ago, they had driven me from these grounds after branding me unstable and dangerous. Only now could I fully grasp what had happened while I was gone. The Grant family was coming apart piece by piece. I breathed in the cold night air. Against the glass, my reflection watched me with silver eyes brightened by resolve. "I won't stand by while they destroy Grandmother's legacy," I whispered. "This time, what belongs to me is coming back into my hands.", Chapter 5: The Door Reopens Elena By the following morning, Grandfather and I stood before the formidable medical building at Seattle University. His hand closed around mine. Determination brightened his silver eyes as he asked, "Are you ready?" I nodded and straightened the plain black blouse I had chosen. Three years earlier, I had imagined entering this building as new medical student. I had finally returned, though nothing about the circumstances resembled that dream. Dean Fletcher's office looked designed to announce his importance. Elaborate furniture crowded the room, expensive art covered the walls, and absurdly broad desk dominated the center. Fletcher himself was a lean, tall man with meticulously arranged salt-and-pepper hair. Beneath his cologne lingered the distinct scent of a natural-born werewolf. His secretary withdrew and shut the door. The instant were alone, Fletcher discarded his polished smile. "Miss Grant, this university admits only the strongest candidates in the region," he said. He made no move to invite us to sit. Grandfather planted both hands on his cane. "My granddaughter finished at the top of her class in Portland, and her medical aptitude scores are outstanding." Coldness settled over Fletcher's features. "Grades and test results aren't our only concerns. Certain other factors must be considered." There it was. I had known he would reach this point. Although no one else could hear us, Fletcher lowered his voice. "People in our community haven't forgotten what happened three years ago, Miss Grant. Accepting a student with your particular... difficulties would create an unacceptable risk." Tension hardened my jaw. "Three years is a long time." "Is it really?" His brows climbed. "We educate the children of influential families here, along with those expected to become our future leaders. Humans attend this institution as well." Grandfather gripped his cane so fiercely that his knuckles lost their color. "This is an outrage. The Grant family has supported this university for generations." "The world has changed, Mr. Grant." Fletcher's reply held no warmth. "Your family no longer possesses the influence it once did." A buzz from his phone interrupted Grandfather before he could answer. Fletcher checked the display, and crease appeared between his brows. "I have to respond to this. Wait here, please." Once he had left the office, I faced Grandfather. "This isn't worth fighting over. I can stay in Portland. Their program is perfectly adequate." "No." His answer came as growl. "Seattle is your home, and this is where you belong." Fletcher returned about five minutes later, but the man who entered seemed nothing like the one who had walked out. His hostility had vanished beneath a strained, accommodating expression. He adjusted his tie before speaking. "I have reconsidered the matter. Miss Grant's transfer application will be approved." Suspicion narrowed my eyes. "What happened while you were gone?" Something uneasy crossed his face and disappeared. "Someone has reminded me that your talents are rather unusual. Apparently, your medical expertise extends to the treatment of certain... specialized injuries." My back went rigid. He could only mean my skill at treating wounds caused by silver bullets, an uncommon ability that made me valuable to injured werewolves. I couldn't imagine how Fletcher had learned about it. He cleared his throat. "There is one condition. You will be assigned to Medical Class Eight, whose students are not considered our strongest performers." Grandfather drew breath to object, but I caught his arm and squeezed. Admission was the important part. A weak class assignment was something I could manage. "I appreciate the opportunity," I said, pressing courtesy into every word. *** That afternoon, a balding human escorted me to Class Eight. Chalk dust and stale coffee clung to his clothes. We traveled to the medical building's most distant corridor, where tired fluorescent tubes blinked above rows of scared desks. He stopped at the front without bothering to conceal his disinterest. "This is Elena Grant. She'll be studying with us beginning today." Thirty students examined me with open suspicion while I delivered a short introduction. Rather than meet their stares, I focused on the rear wall. "Isn't she part of that pack family that was disgraced?" "Supposedly, she did something awful and they threw her out." "Then why come back to Seattle?" No one made much effort to whisper. Four students occupied the back corner, and their werewolf scent identified them immediately. Each of them deliberately looked elsewhere. One spoke just loudly enough for my sharpened hearing. "So the white freak came back." Without reacting, I took the vacant desk beside the window. In Portland, I taught myself most of the material covered by these courses. University policy still requires me to complete several introductory classes before I can receive formal credit. Prescott began a monotonous lecture on cellular structures. Two rows ahead of me, a blonde girl would not stop twisting around to glare in my direction. The moment lunch break arrived, she marched toward my desk with three hostile friends at her back. "Coming here takes a lot of nerve," she announced, making certain the whole room could listen. "You're Elena Grant, aren't you?" I met her stare without warmth. "Who are you supposed to be?" With a dramatic toss of her hair, she said, "Jenna Fairchild. Everybody knows your story. Your own family kicked you out, you started associating with street criminals, and then you got pregnant and aborted the child. You're revolting." My relatives had already banished me over the problems surrounding my transformation. Spreading stories that I had joined criminals was worse, especially when they had carried those lies into the human community. That crossed a boundary even they should have respected. I gathered my books instead of giving her the reaction she wanted. "That's quite an imaginative tale. Did you invent it alone, or did someone help you?" Color surged into her face. "You act like you're above everyone else. People like you make me sick." When I rose, Jenna shifted sideways and sealed off the aisle. "This conversation isn't finished." A thick silver ring gleamed on her finger, only a short distance from my arm. Most humans couldn't recognize werewolves by sight, so they often carried silver jewelry as protection. Jenna might have regarded it as an ordinary accessory, but against my skin it could become a weapon. I eased one step out of reach. "I'm going to the library. Move aside, please." "And if I don't?" She advanced, bringing the ring within inches of me. Around us, every werewolf had gone watchful. They were likely waiting to see whether my control would break. I kept my voice quiet. "I don't intend to cause trouble on my first day. Don't confuse that decision with an inability to defend myself." My tone made Jenna pause. Before she recovered, I slipped around her friends and walked through the door. *** Several hours later, I was speeding along the coastal highway on my Ducati. Wind hammered my leather jacket, and mile by mile, the strain of the day began to loosen. A vibration from my encrypted phone pulsed against my pocket. I stopped at scenic overlook above the Sound, where gulls wheled over the darkening water, and answered the call. "Aria, a new contract just came in," Aaron said. "Do you want it?" "Not at the moment." I watched the birds circle below. "I've only just returned to Seattle, and my real life is already complicated enough." "The money is exceptionally good," he pressed. "More importantly, the client is huge. Hayes Corporation." My grip nearly failed. "Hayes Corporation? You mean DAMIAN HAYES's company?" "Exactly that one. They're searching for somebody with your particular abilities." Questions collided inside my head. Could this job be related to the men who had attacked Damian, or had the timing produced an unlikely coincidence? "Let me consider it," I said at last, then disconnected. I remained beside the highway, staring across the water as daylight faded. What kind of game was DAMIAN HAYES playing? Why was he recruiting both a hacker and werewolves who possessed rare medical expertise? More importantly, had he discovered that the two people he was trying to recruit were both me? Chapter 6: The Aurora Trace Elena The moment I crossed the threshold of the Grant mansion, I wished I had stayed away. Cold elegance filled every corner. Whatever warmth I remembered had vanished, leaving behind an expensive cage disguised as family home. Vanessa and Kendra had positioned themselves in the living room like hunters expecting prey. Disapproval had already settled across Vanessa's face before she spoke. "You come back this late and expect no questions? Where have you been?" Kendra arranged her features into a counterfeit look of concern. "It's not safe to wander around after dark, Sister. You haven't forgotten the rules of this family, have you?" Her performance was so polished that I nearly applauded. Instead, I gave a dry laugh. "You're improving, Kendra. Keep practicing and Hollywood might finally notice you." I turned toward the stairs before either of them could begin a proper interrogation. Behind me, Vanessa raised her voice across the living room. "Just look at her behavior. She's turning the Grant name into a joke throughout the werewolf community." Kendra made certain her reply carried all the way to the staircase. "And after she nearly caused that disaster last time... You remember the incident." My hand tightened around the banister. I kept climbing, denying them reaction they wanted. Hunger eventually forced me out of my room. Downstairs, the kitchen gleamed with unnatural perfection. Every dish had been cleared away, and inspection of the refrigerator revealed bare shelves. They hadn't saved so much as scrap. Vanessa watched from the doorway with folded arms. "We've already had dinner. If you insist on arriving at this hour, feed yourself." As Kendra walked past, she offered me another sugary smile. "Should I make you something?" The amusement in her eyes stripped the kindness from her words. "No need." I kept my voice level despite the ache beneath my ribs. "Looking after myself isn't new to me." Only the fruit bowl had escaped their efforts. I selected an apple and bit into it as if that had been my plan all along. Desperation was another pleasure I refused to hand them. Once I had returned to my bedroom, I opened my modified laptop. Its plain exterior concealed the layered encryption architecture I had built into it myself. Several security protocols came online before I entered the digital world under the identity Aria. Aaron had sent me an alert about possible assault on Hayes Corporation's network. After slipping inside its systems, I needed only minutes to verify the threat: anti-werewolf group was trying to seize information from Hayes's latest medical project. "Of course," I murmured while commands streamed beneath my fingers. "Hatred always finds more work for itself." I cut between the attackers and their target with careful, calculated strikes, then sealed their data routes. The zealots had chosen an opponent they didn't understand. Aria did not lose. After forwarding the intelligence to Aaron, I began wiping away my presence. Before I could finish, my bedroom door crashed open. I snapped the laptop shut. My pulse kicked hard, but I had already caught sight of the warning on the display: someone was attempting to trace the connection. Kendra occupied the doorway without the slightest hint that she should have knocked. Suspicion sharpened her stare. "What exactly are you hiding in here?" "Have you ever considered knocking?" I shoved the computer beneath my pillow. "Why are you here?" Ignoring the question implicit in my tone, she entered and surveyed the room as though conducting an inspection. "Mother wants you at tomorrow's family meeting. Personally, I don't understand why you get a voice in family business after disappearing for three years." I waited until she had finally gone before retrieving the laptop. The screen confirmed my concern. Someone inside Hayes Corporation was attempting to follow Aria's signal to its origin. "Damn it." My hands raced over the keys as I strengthened the defensive layers and destroyed every remaining sign of what I had done. Carelessness had put me in this position. I couldn't keep working as Aria from the Grant estate; the exposure risk was too high. If my hacker identity were uncovered while I lived under this roof, both Grandfather and I would become targets. The solution arrived with brutal clarity. Reclaiming my rightful place in the family required privacy, and privacy meant leaving. I needed a secure base where no one could watch my screen, track my movements, or connect Elena Grant to Aria. I pulled out a suitcase and packed quickly. Clothes and necessities went in first, followed by my hacking equipment. Somewhere beyond this mansion, I could work without fearing an interruption and prepare my next move beyond the family's constant scrutiny. Vanessa intercepted me at the bottom of the stairs and planted herself between me and the exit. "And where do you think you're taking that suitcase?" "Somewhere I can have space of my own." I met her gaze without blinking. "But don't mistake this for surrender. I'm still claiming everything that belongs to me." From the corner, Kendra's mouth curled with satisfaction. "So you're finally going." I answered with an icy look, then walked out. Damian The office door flew open before Security Chief Mason rushed inside. Panic had drained the color from his face. "Mr. Hayes, our central systems are facing a massive attack." I put aside the documents in front of me and followed him at once. By the time we entered the security center, frantic streams of information were racing across the wall display. The system collapse had already advanced to eighty-five percent. Mason pointed toward the cascading alerts. "They've breached three firewall layers. We have only minutes before the core files are exposed." Panic would solve nothing. "Bring every backup defense online and alert the entire security team." "There isn't enough time," he said, shaking his head. "At least twelve elite hackers are attacking together. Our people can't contain them." The files at risk held our most valuable research: medical technology designed to stop silver from injuring werewolves. Should anti-werewolf organization obtain it, the damage could spread far beyond this building. The system hovered on the edge of failure. Then every monitor flickered at once. An aurora unfurled across the primary screen. Mason stared at it. "Aria. That's Aria! The Monglow core member you contacted has actually answered us." The flow of data abruptly changed course. One hostile incursion after another broke apart under a relentless counterattack. Firewall sections rebuilt themselves faster than our monitors could record the process, sealing the core information safely behind them. "That shouldn't be possible," Mason whispered. Awe displaced the panic in his expression. "One hacker just destroyed a coordinated team by herself. We're watching a legend happen in real time." I studied the aurora emblem pulsing on the display. Curiosity tightened into something far more compelling. What kind of person could wield that degree of control from behind a hidden identity? "Find Aria's location and uncover who she is," I said. "I want the signal traced to its source." Mason turned back to his station and worked through the remaining data. His answer came quickly. "The trace only gives us a broad search zone, but we know this much: Aria is here in Seattle." That information focused every instinct I possessed. "Reach out to Monglow. Arrange a personal meeting with Aria. The security of the entire werewolf community may depend on her." When the meeting ended and the others filed out, Elder Rowan remained behind. Privacy did nothing to soften his approach. "Damian, you're thirty-five," he said. "You're also Alpha of Seattle's wolf pack, and Alpha needs a mate." I gave him no visible reaction. "At present, other matters require my attention." His expression hardened. "Without a mate, an Alpha lacks stability. The Council has already begun discussing candidates who could take your position." A dangerous chill moved through me. "Then anyone planning to challenge me had better accept the cost first." Rowan released a weary breath. Shaking his head, he left me alone with the city lights beyond the window. Plenty of werewolf women had pursued me, yet none of them occupied my thoughts as I looked over Seattle. Instead, my mind returned to the mysterious white wolf: Elena Grant. Her silver-gray gaze. Her rare white-wolf lineage. The medical talent that set her apart from everyone around her. No matter what I did, I couldn't force her out of my mind. I didn't understand why.
