adCopy: After my mom died, my brother took the dining set. My sister took the china cabinet. I took nine shoeboxes and for a year I couldn't explain why to anyone... Not even to myself, honestly. This was 14 months ago, the weekend after Mom's funeral. The three of us walking through her house with little colored stickers, putting our names on furniture like it wasn't the saddest thing we'd ever done. And in the hall closet, on the top shelf where she kept them my whole life, nine shoeboxes of photographs. My brother looked at them and said "what do we even do with those." Not a question. Just... a shrug with words on it. So I took them. All nine. Loaded them in my trunk between a lamp and her sewing machine and drove them home to my own hall closet, where they sat. And sat. Here's what nobody tells you about inheriting the family photos: you don't inherit photos. You inherit a job. Almost 3,000 pictures going back to 1954. Her wedding. My grandparents on the porch of a house that got torn down in the 70s. My dad in his Army uniform, 22 years old. Me and my siblings in matching Easter outfits Mom sewed herself. Every single one of them exists in exactly ONE place on this earth. One water heater leak. One basement flood. One house fire and it's not like losing pictures, it's like everyone dies a second time. I thought about that constantly. I'd check on the boxes like they were a sleeping baby. Actually moved them to the top shelf of my bedroom closet because I read that's safer in a flood. My daughter thought I was losing it a little. Maybe I was. So I did what you're supposed to do. I called one of those photo scanning services... The nice young man quoted me $847 for the whole collection. Plus shipping. And you have to MAIL them your photos. Put the only copies of your mother's entire life in a cardboard box and hand them to the postal service and just... hope. I couldn't do it. Hung up and felt sick. Then I tried doing it myself, because how hard could it be. Bought a flatbed scanner for $109. Timed myself the first night: about four minutes a photo by the time you place it, scan it, name the file, save it somewhere. Four minutes times 3,000 photos. I did the math at the kitchen table and it came out to over 190 hours. I scanned 41 photos and never opened the thing again. It's in the garage right now if anybody wants it. Then I tried just taking pictures of the pictures with my phone, which sounds smart until you see the glare. Every photo had a big white stripe from the ceiling light. My grandmother's face, glare. Dad's uniform, glare. So I did the thing I'm most ashamed of. Nothing. For almost a year, I did nothing. The boxes sat in my closet and I just quietly carried it around, this low hum of "if anything ever happens..." Then in February my sister called asking if I could send her the photo of Dad holding her at the hospital, 1961, because it was her birthday and she wanted to post it. And I had to say no. Not "no I don't have it." No, I can't GET it to you. It's in a box, in a closet, in another state, and there's no copy. She was sweet about it. That made it worse somehow. Now here's where this turns, and I want you to know the discovery was a complete accident. For Christmas my daughter gave me this little gadget called Clickfree. And she didn't buy it for the shoeboxes at all... she bought it because my PHONE had been saying storage full for two years and I kept just clicking the notification away. It's about the size of a pack of gum. You plug it into your phone, press one button, and it copies everything onto the drive itself. Photos, videos, even my contacts. Took a few minutes. Cleared years of guilt off my phone in one sitting, fine, great, thank you honey. But that night I'm sitting in bed poking around the app and I see a feature that says you can scan printed photos with it. I actually said "no it can't" out loud. Alone. In my bedroom. Because here's what it claims: you point your phone camera at an old printed photo, and it scans it, crops it, straightens it, and saves it to the drive. No scanner. No glare stripe. No mailing your mother's life to a warehouse. I got out of bed at 11-something at night, got a shoebox down, and tried it on the Easter photo. It just... did it. Cropped it clean, squared it up, saved it. Looked better than anything that $109 flatbed scanner gave me, and it took seconds instead of four minutes. I did about 60 photos that first night sitting on my bedroom floor like a teenager. Went to bed at 1 AM. Sixty-three years old. And then it became my winter. Sunday afternoons, coffee, one shoebox at a time. Some weeks I did 200, some weeks 40. By March I had every single photo, all nine boxes, on this little drive that lives in my fireproof document bag now. Not on some company's server where I'm renting my own memories for $2.99 a month until they get hacked or lock me out. On a drive. That I own. In my house. It doesn't even need internet, which frankly is the part that sold my brother when I showed him. But none of that is why I'm writing this. There's a feature in there I didn't touch for weeks because it sounded like a gimmick. AI photo enhancement. It says it can fix blur, correct colors... and colorize black and white photos. My parents got married in 1958. The only photos of that day are black and white. And my whole life, my mother told the same story: that her wedding dress was pale blue. Not white, blue. She'd say "you can't tell in the pictures, but it was blue like a robin's egg." Her mother thought it was a scandal. It was her favorite story about herself. I never saw the dress. It got lost in a move before I was born. You already know what I did. I sat at my kitchen table with the wedding photo and pressed the colorize button, and I watched my mother turn 20 years old in front of me, standing next to my father in his one good suit... In a pale blue dress. Blue like a robin's egg. I called my sister and couldn't get the first sentence out. Just crying and going "the dress. The dress." She thought something was wrong with me. I mailed her a print of it. She has it framed in her hallway. Dad holding her in 1961 is on her fridge now too, because that one took me about ten seconds to send once it was on the drive. I'm not going to sit here and tell you every old photo comes out like a miracle. A couple of really faded ones from the 50s came out just okay for me. But okay beats gone. And that's really the whole thing I keep coming back to. Nobody teaches you what to do with the boxes. The scanning companies want hundreds of dollars and your originals in the mail. The cloud companies want rent, forever, on your own family. And so the photos just sit in closets all over the country, one bad day from disappearing, while everybody shrugs and says "what do we even do with those." Now when people ask me, I have an answer. I'm not going to tell you what to do. But if there's a closet in your house, or your mom's house, with boxes like mine in it... I'd at least go look at this thing. It was one of those situations where they had a 50% off deal and a 30-day money back guarantee when my daughter bought mine, so she figured worst case she'd return it. She didn't return it. Nine shoeboxes are still in my closet, by the way. I couldn't throw them out, they still smell like her house. But now they're just boxes. Everything inside them is safe.

adCopy: My Wife Had Tinnitus So Bad She Stopped Coming To Bed. This Year's Gift Was Thirty Seconds Behind Her Ear. I'm Mark. I'm 61. Carol is 58. I need to tell you what the ringing did to our nights, because for a long time I thought she was mad at me. She wasn't mad. She could not stand the quiet. The quiet made the sound louder. Fan. Hallway light. Phone under the pillow with a rain track. None of it won. She got it after years of classrooms. Thirty kids. Whistles. A fire alarm that went off wrong one semester and sat in her head afterward. Or that is the story we tell. The ENT did not give us a cleaner one. Hearing fine for her age. Then the sentence. "You'll just have to learn to live with it." So she learned. She stopped going to restaurants with hard floors. She stopped the movie theater. She started going to bed an hour after me so she would not have to explain why she needed the TV on at a whisper that still was not enough. I bought her things. Ginkgo. Magnesium. A lipo something from the pharmacy aisle. A white noise machine shaped like a stone. A pair of headphones she hated. Anniversary. Birthday. Christmas. I kept buying the cover-up. Last fall I almost did it again. A nicer machine. Holiday sale. Then I read about a nerve behind the ear that can get stuck ON. The auricular nerve. It is supposed to report real sound. A door. A voice. A car horn. When it is damaged — noise, stress, age, infection — it can keep firing with nothing there. Phantom signals. A fire alarm that had a reason once. Then the reason left. And the alarm stayed. That is her ringing. Not a mystery personality. A nerve that will not stand down. Pills cannot aim at one nerve behind the ear. They go through the stomach and hope. White noise does not fix it. It stacks sound. Turn it off and the hiss is waiting. The thing that actually calms that kind of misfire in clinic settings is neuromuscular stimulation. NMS. Tiny low-frequency pulses. Same broad idea you see in pain management and physical therapy. When studies aimed NMS at the auricular nerve, they reported reduced phantom ringing in up to 98% of participants. Not a new noise. A signal to stop. Those machines cost a thousand dollars or more. Sometimes three. Appointments. Drive time. Insurance theater. I am not a rich man. I am a husband who was about to wrap another speaker. I sat with that for three days before I clicked. Because I have been the man who buys things and hopes. Because she has been the woman who unwraps them and pretends. Because eleven Decembers of covering a nerve with a bow will make you careful. I read the page twice. Auricular nerve. Stuck ON. NMS. Thirty seconds. 30-day money back. I thought about the clinical machines I could not drive her to every week. I thought about the $400 program that taught her to "reframe" a sound that was still screaming. Reframing is not an off button. I ordered Tinnito instead. I ordered Tinnito instead. It looks like a pen. You hold it behind the ear for about thirty seconds. Press. A gentle pulse. That is the whole ritual. Carol called it a gadget. I put it in a box with a bow anyway. Early. Not even Christmas yet. I could not watch another month of her staring at the ceiling. She tried it the first night to humor me. I stayed in the kitchen. When she came out she did not cry. She does not cry easy. She said, "The volume dropped." Like a radio tuned down. Not off. Down. She did it again the next morning. By the end of the week she came to bed when I did. I kept a stupid little log on my phone. Not for science. For me. Day one. Volume dropped. She said it like she was afraid to jinx it. Day four. She turned the hallway light off. That light had been a night-light for the ringing. Day nine. She laughed at something on the couch and did not stop to say "what?" Day fourteen. Guest bed sheets washed and folded. Not because we had guests. Because she did not need that room anymore. By the end of the week she came to bed when I did. The TV stayed off. I want to be straight. Some days it ticks up. A loud cafeteria. A bad sinus week. But the house is not run by the hiss anymore. She went to a restaurant last month. Hard floors. She stayed. She sat through a whole movie. Our son noticed before I said anything. "Mom's not doing the what-what thing." That was his whole review. If your wife leaves the room when it gets quiet. If she sleeps in the guest bed with a machine going and still loses. If an ENT handed her those five words and you both nodded because you did not know what else to do. If you have already bought the pills and the apps and the stone-shaped speaker. If Q4 is here and you were about to order another cover-up with a bow on it. Stop. The gift is not more noise. The gift is a way to tell the nerve to stand down. Xeviola's Tinnito puts that clinic-style NMS idea into a home pen. On their page it is 60% off with free shipping when the launch price is live — less than forty dollars. They frame the full price near a hundred. Clinical units are thousands. 30 days. Try it. Every penny back if nothing moves. https://xeviola.com/products/tinnito Thirty seconds behind the ear. I almost bought the wrong gift again. I am glad I didn't. Holiday gift guides will sell you candles and robes and another gadget that hums. None of those touch a nerve stuck in the ON position. If your wife has started living in the next room over so she can survive the quiet, do not buy her more quiet-noise. Buy her a way to turn the real noise down. Thirty seconds. Behind the ear. A pen. That is a Christmas morning that does not end in a polite thank-you and a return to the guest bed. ~ Mark Delaney, 61 P.S. The stone speaker is in the closet. She has not asked for it. I leave it there so I remember what I used to wrap. P.P.S. If you get two, the page makes multi-unit cheaper. Her sister teaches too. Same cafeteria roar. That is a better December than candles. P.P.P.S. She still says it is not a miracle. She says it is quieter. Quieter was enough to come back to bed. P.P.P.P.S. I used to think a good husband fixed things with purchases. More machines. More bottles. More hope in a box. A good husband finds the actual switch. The auricular nerve was the switch. The pen reaches it. The bow was optional. If your wife has tinnitus and Q4 is breathing down your neck, do not wait for Christmas morning to be brave. Order it. Let her try it under the 30-day window. If it does nothing, you send it back and you still have time for the robe. If it drops the volume, you already gave her the only gift she has been asking for without asking. Let me say the fork plainly. One path: another Christmas morning with a polite smile and a machine that hums while the nerve keeps screaming. Another path: a pen, a thirty-second ritual, a 30-day window, and a wife who comes back to bed because the quiet is quiet again. I am 61. I am not fancy. I just stopped buying cover-ups. If her tinnitus has been the third person in your marriage, this is the year you send that person packing. https://xeviola.com/products/tinnito Hold it behind her ear. Watch what happens to the night. Men are bad at saying this part, so I will say it plain. I missed my wife. Not the roommate who managed a ringing head. My wife. The one who falls asleep on my shoulder during a movie. The one who does not flinch when the house goes silent. Tinnitus had been taking pieces of her evenings for years while I kept shopping for accessories to the problem. This Q4 I shopped for the problem itself. Thirty seconds behind her ear. A pen from Xeviola called Tinnito. 60% off when the offer is live. Free shipping. 30 days to reverse it. If you love her, stop decorating the coping. https://xeviola.com/products/tinnito Order it like you mean the holidays. P.P.P.P.P.S. If she opens it and laughs, good. Let her laugh. Then ask her to try it once before bed. The laugh is not the review. The morning after is. I already bought the wrong gifts. This one earned the bow.
